strengths: The proposed TAG update is simple, inexpensive, and easy to insert after an existing sampler step: it decomposes the latent update into radial and tangential components and amplifies only the tangential part, adding negligible runtime and no extra model evaluations.

The manuscript provides a coherent geometric intuition and includes both unconditional and conditional variants, with experiments across SD v1.5, SD v2.1, SDXL, SD3/flow matching, DDIM, DPM++, and combinations with SAG/PAG/SEG.

The empirical tables show consistent FID/IS improvements in several matched-compute settings, and the ablation on the amplification parameter eta usefully shows that moderate amplification helps while excessive amplification degrades quality.
The paper acknowledges an important limitation: eta must be tuned, and large eta perturbs the sampler's radial calibration.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is overstated. The monotonicity theorem mostly follows from defining the update to scale a component aligned with the model score under a first-order approximation; it does not establish improvement in true data likelihood, hallucination resistance, semantic correctness, or sample quality. The proof relies on approximating the true score by the learned score and ignores higher-order terms that the paper later admits can dominate for larger eta.

The method's novelty is somewhat incremental relative to recent geometry-aware and tangential guidance work, especially tangential damping CFG and other projection-based guidance methods. The paper does not sufficiently clarify why amplifying tangential components is fundamentally distinct from or preferable to these closely related approaches.

The evaluation is not yet convincing enough for acceptance. FID values for SD-based ImageNet generation are very high, suggesting an unusual or weak evaluation setup, and the paper does not compare against several strong or directly relevant inference-time guidance baselines such as limited-interval guidance, bad-version guidance, TCFG-style methods, or tuned CFG variants.

Conditional-generation results are mixed despite the positive framing: PAG+C-TAG and SEG+C-TAG improve FID but reduce CLIPScore, with SEG dropping substantially, which weakens the claim that text-image alignment is largely preserved. The comparison using different NFEs/steps for CFG and C-TAG is also difficult to interpret cleanly.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML main-track paper. The reproducibility statement only names PyTorch and Diffusers; it omits code release details, exact prompts or class-conditioning protocol, seeds, preprocessing specifics, hyperparameter search procedure for eta, scheduler settings, and confidence intervals or variance for FID/IS.

The paper repeatedly frames the contribution as reducing hallucinations, but most evidence uses generic image-quality metrics and qualitative examples. There is no targeted hallucination benchmark, human evaluation, compositionality test, anatomical artifact measurement, or failure-case analysis sufficient to support that central claim.

Presentation is generally readable but sometimes imprecise: terminology such as normal/tangential to the data manifold versus the latent-sphere radius is conflated, the project page footnote appears blank, and some claims such as 'highest similarity to ground truth' or 'SOTA models' are broader than the evidence supports.

Ethical and limitations treatment is incomplete. The paper has a short technical limitation about eta but does not discuss misuse risks, dataset/model licensing, potential amplification of biases in pretrained generative models, or the broader implications of improving image generation fidelity.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple plug-and-play inference-time modification: decompose each sampler update into a component parallel to the current latent and an orthogonal/tangential component, then amplify the tangential part. The implementation is lightweight and plausibly adds little overhead.

The empirical tables show fairly consistent FID/IS improvements over the authors' own baselines across several samplers/backbones, and the ablation over the amplification factor eta correctly notes degradation when eta is too large.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes pseudocode for both unconditional TAG and a conditional variant, plus a limitations section acknowledging sensitivity to eta.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is weak and arguably circular. Theorem 4.1 proves monotonic improvement only for a first-order Taylor gain after replacing the true score by the same model score used in the update. Under this approximation, increasing eta gives an almost tautological larger inner product with the modeled score, but this does not establish movement toward the true data manifold, reduced hallucination, or better final sample quality. The result is also unbounded in eta while the experiments show large eta hurts, so the theorem does not support the practical claim without substantial second-order/scheduler analysis.

The method's originality is insufficiently established. The work is very close in spirit to existing geometry-aware guidance and tangential CFG/damping methods cited by the authors, especially Kwon et al. 2025 and Sadat et al. 2025, but there is no direct comparison to the most relevant tangential guidance baseline or careful discussion of what is genuinely new beyond changing the sign from damping to amplification or applying a projection post-step.

The experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the claims. Absolute unconditional FIDs for SD v1.5/v2.1/SDXL/SD3 on ImageNet are extremely poor, making it unclear whether the setting is meaningful for evaluating hallucination-resistant sampling. The paper does not include standard diversity/precision-recall metrics, human preference studies, artifact/hallucination-specific measurements, confidence intervals, or enough seeds to assess robustness.

Several empirical comparisons are potentially unfair or under-specified. Hyperparameters appear selected per method/backbone without a tuning protocol; baselines are not shown with comparable tuning budgets; conditional CFG+C-TAG is compared at very different step counts; and improvements are mostly reported against weak baselines. The claimed preservation of text-image alignment is contradicted by Table 4, where CLIPScore drops for PAG+C-TAG and SEG+C-TAG.

The conditional formulation is confusing and internally inconsistent. Equation 18 writes CFG as epsilon_c + omega(epsilon_c - epsilon_u), while Algorithm 2 uses epsilon_u + omega g. Equation 20 and Algorithm 2 also differ in how the TAG term is expressed. This makes the actual conditional method hard to verify from the paper.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The reproducibility statement only says PyTorch and Diffusers were used. There is no code release, no exact model checkpoints/settings, no preprocessing details beyond metric package names, no seed list, no hardware-complete runtime setup, and the project-page footnote appears blank. The appendix pseudocode is helpful but not sufficient for reliable reproduction.

The paper lacks an ethics or societal impact discussion despite working on generative image models and hallucination reduction. It also does not discuss possible misuse, bias, or whether improving fidelity may worsen downstream harms.

Presentation has multiple issues that reduce confidence: several qualitative claims rely on small, hard-to-inspect figures; some captions/citations appear wrong or inconsistent, such as SD3 being associated with Podell et al. in Figure 6; and key terms like hallucination, OOD, and semantic coherence are used broadly without operational definitions or targeted evaluation.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing inference-time modification: decompose the sampler update into radial and tangential components relative to the current latent, then amplify only the tangential component. This is easy to implement, architecture-agnostic, and adds essentially no extra denoiser evaluations.

The empirical results are consistently positive across several settings: unconditional SD v1.5, SD v2.1, SDXL, SD3/flow matching, and combinations with SAG/PAG/SEG/CFG. The reported FID/IS/CLIPScore trends support the claim that moderate tangential amplification can improve sample quality at matched or reduced NFEs.

The paper gives useful intuition connecting mode interpolation, Tweedie-style score geometry, and radius-preserving updates. The ablation over the amplification factor eta and the discussion of degradation at large eta are helpful and make the method’s behavior more understandable.

The method is practical and potentially useful: it is plug-and-play, computationally lightweight, and compatible with existing guidance methods. The included pseudocode and implementation snippets are enough to convey the core algorithm.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is weaker than the claims suggest. The monotonic first-order Taylor gain result largely follows from approximating the true score by the model score and from the algebraic form of the DDIM update; it does not establish that samples become more faithful to the true data distribution, nor that hallucinations are reduced beyond a local first-order surrogate.

Several central terms are somewhat overstated. The paper repeatedly claims movement toward higher-density regions and reduced hallucination, but the experiments mostly measure FID/IS/CLIPScore rather than hallucination-specific or semantic consistency metrics. Qualitative examples help, but they do not fully substantiate the stronger hallucination claims.

The evaluation is broad but not fully rigorous. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics for FID/IS, hyperparameter selection for eta appears manual, and comparisons may be sensitive to sampler, timestep schedule, and guidance scale choices. Some conditional results also show tradeoffs, e.g. PAG/SEG with C-TAG improve FID but reduce CLIPScore.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper states the use of PyTorch, Diffusers, fixed seeds, and metric implementations, and gives pseudocode, but it lacks full details on prompts, exact preprocessing, hyperparameter search, model checkpoints/configurations, and whether code will be released.

The presentation is generally understandable but occasionally imprecise. There are formatting issues, incomplete project-page information, inconsistent notation between TAG and C-TAG, and some claims such as “foundational benefits” or “guaranteed to improve” are stronger than the evidence warrants.

The limitations section is honest about eta sensitivity and radial perturbation, but it does not discuss broader risks or failure modes, such as possible diversity loss, prompt-alignment degradation, dataset/model dependence, or the ethical implications of improving image generation fidelity.
